title: HybridQC: Hardware-Grounded Simulation of Tightly Integrated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical performance depends on how quantum processors share classical compute, controllers, memory, and communication links. Circuit simulators and provider measurements expose kernel and job behavior, but leave topology-level questions about controller bottlenecks, quantum capacity, and mixed-workload contention unanswered. We present HybridQC, a discrete-event simulator for configurable hybrid compute units (HCUs). Users specify resource graphs containing classical compute, memory, controllers, quantum annealing (QA) and digital quantum computing (DQC) devices, and links. Jobs become dependent stages for preparation, quantum execution, transfers, reconstruction, and postprocessing. Finite capacities and selectable scheduling policies determine where stages wait and overlap. Service profiles use measurements from D-Wave Advantage 1 and Advantage 2 and IBM Kingston, Marrakesh, and Fez, separating physical quantum-processor occupancy from cloud wall time. Mean absolute percentage errors are 3.92%-8.04% for D-Wave access time and 5.26%-19.01% for IBM quantum seconds. Balanced 10x HCU scaling improves makespan by 2.19x-3.42x, while policy choice changes makespan by 1.80x for a mixed workload with 20 jobs per workload family. Scaling depends on which inputs grow: 100x data growth yields median runtime near 306 s, while 100x joint growth in circuits, shots, and depth reaches 4.806 x 10^7 s on the fixed HCU. HybridQC enables designers to study topology, scheduling, and workload growth before tightly integrated quantum-classical machines exist physically.

title: Political stance detection on X during the 2024 U.S. election: a comparative study of classical, neural, and transformer models
abstract: Abstract As online social networks (OSNs) play an increasingly influential role in political communication, accurately detecting political stance from noisy, short-form content remains a significant challenge in computational social science (CSS). This paper presents a controlled comparison of text classification models for political stance detection during the 2024 U.S. presidential election, focusing on candidate affiliation toward Donald Trump and Joe Biden–Kamala Harris. Using nearly 100,000 posts from X, we define candidate affiliation as a three-class target variable (Trump, Biden–Kamala, or Neutral) and use topic modeling to support keyword development and thematic characterization. Under a unified preprocessing, labeling, and evaluation pipeline, we compare classical machine learning models, sentence-embedding-based neural architectures, and a domain-adapted transformer. Results suggest that task-aligned text representation accounts for most of the predictive signal in this setting. While fine-tuned BERTweet achieves the strongest in-domain performance, carefully engineered classical models, particularly linear support vector machines, remain highly competitive. Multi-feature and ablation analyses further indicate that expanded metadata did not yield reliable gains beyond strong text representations. Overall, this work provides a controlled comparison of text models for candidate affiliation on a heuristically labeled corpus.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Financial Foundation Models: A Survey
abstract: Financial foundation models increasingly support workflows spanning financial question answering, disclosure analysis, forecasting, and decision-making. In these settings, uncertainty may concern whether evidence is valid and available at the relevant time, whether an interpretation is justified, which outcomes remain plausible, or which action is preferred under costs and risk constraints. Because these objects arise at different points in a workflow, uncertainty cannot be reduced to confidence in a final output. We introduce a source-aware framework that distinguishes six sources of uncertainty across evidence and context, model and inference, and outcome and action, while treating agentic workflows as the execution layer through which uncertainty can propagate, change form, or be reduced. We develop a mechanism-based taxonomy grounded in how methods construct or verify uncertainty and reliability representations, and use it to assess their applicability across financial task domains. We further map finance-specific empirical studies across the taxonomy and task domains to characterize the current research landscape. Our analysis shows that most reviewed studies address uncertainty in individual parts of financial workflows, with limited work connecting evidence and reasoning reliability to downstream prediction and constrained action. By connecting where uncertainty arises, how it is represented, and how it bears on downstream decisions, this survey provides a unified foundation for studying and evaluating uncertainty in financial foundation models.

title: Data underlaying chapter 7 to the dissertation 'Expanding Regulatory Sandboxes: Exploring institutional dynamics of hydrogen market development and governance in the Netherlands'
abstract: Research data for Chapter 7 in the dissertation 'Expanding Regulatory Sandboxes: Exploring institutional dynamics of hydrogen market development and governance in the Netherlands'The chapter title is: Serious Gaming and agent-based modelling as a proof of concept for virtual regulatory sandboxes The research objective is to establish a practical approach for using serious gaming as a structured behavioral data eleicitation method, to support ABM development. Through a case study, the pratcical approach is illustrated. This involved the execution of 12 serious game sessions (the hychain serious game) and the collection of behavioral and institutional mechanisms. The collection took place through observation, recording and transcription of each session and the analysis of the collected rules for the number of occurrences. The collected data and corresponding analysis are presented in the attached file. The attached file specifies the data of the game session, the governmental strategy in the session, the corresponding round, the governmental decision taken, the decisions made by actors, the interactions taking place, the individuals involved and a description of the decision or interaction.

title: Faithfulness Under Pressure: Evaluating Hallucination Detectors for Financial RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used in financial applications where generated answers must be grounded in specific documents, filings, or disclosures. Yet even with relevant context, answers may contradict, overextend, or misinterpret the supplied evidence. This paper presents a comparative study of intrinsic hallucination detection for financial RAG, where the task is to determine whether an answer is faithful to a supplied question–context pair. We evaluate DSPy-based prompt optimization, fine-tuned detectors, encoder-based detectors, and LLM-as-Judge frameworks across public benchmarks and finance-specific settings. To examine finance-specific behavior, we construct FinDER-HD, a balanced hallucination-detection benchmark derived from FinDER by synthesizing unfaithful counterparts for faithful financial question–context–answer examples. We further evaluate filing-scale robustness on PHANTOM, which varies context length, evidence position, and filing type. Results show that detector performance varies substantially across datasets, financial topics, reasoning types, and context regimes. DSPy-based prompt optimization is competitive under limited supervision, but robustness differs markedly by optimization strategy: demonstration-heavy methods perform strongly in short contexts yet degrade more sharply as context grows, whereas COPRO and especially GEPA remain substantially more stable. Selected LLM-as-Judge methods also perform strongly in finance-specific settings, but their operating behavior depends on threshold choice and prediction bias. These findings motivate deployment-oriented evaluation of financial RAG guardrails beyond aggregate F1, including finance-specific robustness, filing-scale stress testing, prediction bias, threshold calibration, and context-window feasibility.

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events
abstract: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.

title: EntangledEdge: A Distributed System for Orbital Quantum Sensing and Learning
abstract: An orbital quantum sensor is more precise than classical and holds its information in a quantum state's superposition and entanglement, which classical measurement collapses. Learning on quantum-sensed data therefore requires a distributed system in which the data stay quantum from sensor to inference. We present EntangledEdge, the first system architecture to unify orbital quantum sensing and learning end-to-end, with a quantum data plane and a classical control plane. It routes each event to a channel-matched model in a capacity-diverse bank, adapts its detection threshold without labels, and aggregates across stations by hardware fidelity. Evaluated with a hybrid prototype (real quantum processors, simulated orbit-to-ground link) over satellite telemetry, EntangledEdge achieves high-quality inference at bounded per-event cost, improves quantum processor utilization, and scales with fleet size.

title: CARTA: Self-Supervised Reusable Transaction Embeddings via Heterogeneous Tokenization and Cross-Attention
abstract: Acquiring fraud labels for payment transactions is expensive and inconsistent across tasks, and high-cardinality identifiers such as merchant names make one-hot feature pipelines infeasible at scale. We present CARTA, a self-supervised encoder that learns a compact 16-dim embedding from raw transactions without labels; the frozen embedding is then reused for label-efficient fraud probing and exploratory unsupervised risk stratification without retraining the encoder. CARTA uses type-specific projections with learned embedding tables for high-cardinality identifiers, trained with token excision and InfoNCE contrastive loss. On IEEE-CIS, its linear probe at 1% of labels exceeds a raw-feature probe at 100%; on IBM TabFormer (2M rows), its frozen embedding reaches GBDT AUPRC 0.508, above frequency encoding (0.411) and the merchant-dropping baseline (0.022), though fully-supervised CatBoost is stronger. CARTA is a label-free, reusable representation that complements task-specific supervised models.

title: Decodability Is Not Validity: Evaluating Nuisance Sensitivity in Language Model Concept Probes
abstract: Two concept probes can be equally accurate at predicting a concept from a language model’s hidden states while their scores contain different mixtures of the target concept and a correlated nuisance attribute. In four target–nuisance settings (two aspect sentiments in CEBaB; occupation and gender in BiasBios; Amazon review sentiment with negation, and with firstperson framing), two LLMs, and a population of concept extractors, we compare decodability with discriminant evidence: the score’s dependence on the nuisance at fixed target, and its response to input edits intended to change only the nuisance, filtered by two LLM judges and compared against placebo edits. Under correlated training data, extractors that are statistically equivalent in held-out AUROC differ up to several-fold in nuisance sensitivity in three of the four settings, and decodability is not a reliable proxy for it: their rank correlation changes sign across settings. The effect follows the probe’s training data, not the nuisance’s natural association with the target: first-person framing, unrelated to sentiment in natural reviews, is absorbed at least as much as negation, which co-occurs with negative sentiment, and decorrelated training removes the systematic effect. Selecting extractors with nuisance-aware development diagnostics, which need nuisance labels but no counterfactuals, lowers counterfactual nuisance sensitivity wherever the default choice is sensitive, at a small accuracy cost. Concept measurements should be validated, not just decoded.

title: Nepali-English Code-Mixed Speech Recognition: Data Preparation and Adaptation of a Speech Foundation Model
abstract: Nepali speakers regularly mix English words into conversation, but multilingual speech recognisers often struggle with language switches and the writing script used for English words. We study how to adapt SraVaani, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, using a 172.8-hour corpus covering six Nepali speech domains. Its pretrained tokenizer does not support digits and several common symbols. Rather than replace it or discard these recordings, we generate Nepali and English readings for numbers and use zero-shot ASR output to select a plausible form. Full fine-tuning reduces test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%; a 12-epoch run reaches 16.3%, compared with 16.4% for fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo. Freezing the encoder increases WER to 25.5%, while excluding numeric clips raises WER on numeric test speech from 14.3% to 21.3%. We also evaluate on FLEURS using both its original references and mixed-script alternatives. The comparison shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain performance loss.

title: 具身智能动作决策的最小证据边界 / Minimal Evidence Boundaries for Action Decisions in Embodied Agents
abstract: 本稿为中文方法与理论研究草稿,提出以当前动作是否可被证据确认,作为进一步获取观测的停止条件。稿件区分静态离线最短证书与在线自适应查询代价,并给出基本推导、动态失效反例与后续比较实验方案。研究仍处于探索阶段,新颖性与实际工程收益尚未建立;本文不是经同行评审的期刊论文。 Minimal Evidence Boundaries for Action Decisions in Embodied Agents. This Chinese-language methods and theory draft studies action-specific evidence acquisition, distinguishing offline certificates from online adaptive query costs. It includes elementary propositions, a dynamic invalidation counterexample, and a falsifiable evaluation plan. Novelty and practical benefits remain to be established. This is an exploratory preprint, not a peer-reviewed journal article. Validation is limited to a four-bit static logical model: 16 worlds, 81 partial-evidence states and 256 compatible world/evidence pairs. The included standard-library Python program and actual JSON output reproduce these checks. There are no physical robot experiments, learned-model benchmarks or claims of real-world safety. Query-count comparisons apply only to the stated toy model and uniform distribution. Files: six-page Chinese manuscript PDF, editable DOCX, Python checker, actual enumeration results and reproduction instructions. Manuscript version completed on 2026-11-13; repository publication date is 2026-11-14. The manuscript's statement that it had not yet been submitted describes its status when written. AI assistance was used for ideation, literature discovery, drafting, formalization, coding and typesetting. Related work and limitations are explicitly discussed. The listed author and affiliation follow author-provided information: YANGZHOU, 梗必爆具身交互AI研究院 (Genbibao Embodied AI Research Institute), ORCID 0009-0005-4736-2097. This record does not assert journal acceptance or indexing by CNKI or Scopus.

title: Coverage Beats Chronology: Distilling Tabular Foundation Models for Drifting, Rare-Event Financial Risk
abstract: Distilling a tabular foundation model (TFM) into a CPU-deployable tree is established practice on IID benchmarks, where retention of the teacher’s absolute accuracy exceeds 95%, but financial risk breaks that setting twice over: the data are temporally ordered, and a gradient-boosted baseline is strong enough that the teacher’s edge is only an increment, so absolute retention stays high even when nothing useful transfers. We therefore report gain retention, Rgain, the fraction of the teacher’s advantage over a matched labels-only student that survives compression, and we factorially vary the one choice a practitioner must make: how the teacher’s soft targets are built. On frozen test windows of five temporal fraud streams (Bank Account Fraud with two bias variants, IEEE-CIS and Elliptic), a student scoring a row in 0.52 ms on one CPU core (107 × the teacher’s batched throughput) retains 96% of the teacher’s incremental advantage at a 16K-label budget (+ 8.7 pp PR-AUC). The decisive design choice is target coverage, not chronology: on BAF’s development window, labelling every available row is worth + 3.03 pp against + 0.50 pp for the construction protocol, and forward chaining, the temporally cautious scheme most practitioners reach for, is unnecessary and costs up to 3.5 pp; on frozen test windows the coverage advantage holds in all four replication streams (median + 0.97 pp over 12 cells). That advantage is conditional, and we quantify the condition: across 12 frozen-test stream–budget cells it grows with the teacher’s margin over a matched labels-only tree (r = 0.79), and where a tree already matches the foundation model the selector discards the teacher in 10 of 12 runs, making the choice moot by construction. The calibration cost that appears to accompany distillation is an artifact of temperature-scaled targets, not a property of the teacher, and inverts at no cost to ranking.

evidence.title: Coverage Beats Chronology: Distilling Tabular Foundation Models for Drifting, Rare-Event Financial Risk
evidence.abstract: Distilling a tabular foundation model (TFM) into a CPU-deployable tree is established practice on IID benchmarks, where retention of the teacher’s absolute accuracy exceeds 95%, but financial risk breaks that setting twice over: the data are temporally ordered, and a gradient-boosted baseline is strong enough that the teacher’s edge is only an increment, so absolute retention stays high even when nothing useful transfers. We therefore report gain retention, Rgain, the fraction of the teacher’s advantage over a matched labels-only student that survives compression, and we factorially vary the one choice a practitioner must make: how the teacher’s soft targets are built. On frozen test windows of five temporal fraud streams (Bank Account Fraud with two bias variants, IEEE-CIS and Elliptic), a student scoring a row in 0.52 ms on one CPU core (107 × the teacher’s batched throughput) retains 96% of the teacher’s incremental advantage at a 16K-label budget (+ 8.7 pp PR-AUC). The decisive design choice is target coverage, not chronology: on BAF’s development window, labelling every available row is worth + 3.03 pp against + 0.50 pp for the construction protocol, and forward chaining, the temporally cautious scheme most practitioners reach for, is unnecessary and costs up to 3.5 pp; on frozen test windows the coverage advantage holds in all four replication streams (median + 0.97 pp over 12 cells). That advantage is conditional, and we quantify the condition: across 12 frozen-test stream–budget cells it grows with the teacher’s margin over a matched labels-only tree (r = 0.79), and where a tree already matches the foundation model the selector discards the teacher in 10 of 12 runs, making the choice moot by construction. The calibration cost that appears to accompany distillation is an artifact of temperature-scaled targets, not a property of the teacher, and inverts at no cost to ranking.

title: A Governance Control-Plane for Agentic AI in Regulated Financial Systems: A Fraud-Detection Case Study
abstract: We propose a governance control-plane for agentic AI in regulated financial services: an agent-agnostic layer combining a bounded-autonomy policy engine, a hash-chained audit trail, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) gate, a dual-signal drift monitor (PSI + chi-squared), a kill switch, and a structured evidence-faithfulness check. Two findings stand out. First, confidence-based PSI completely misses a prompt-induced behavioral shift in Llama 3 while a post-hoc chi-squared decision-proportion test localizes the shift within 80 transactions of injection – empirical motivation for the dual-signal design, although online detection of this failure mode remains open. Second, 51% of escalations breach the 90-second SLA under realistic reviewer latency, motivating a re-queue policy that reduces permanent holds by 76.3%. Against a fail-open ungoverned baseline, the governed system raises recall from 49.1% to 92.6% (stability confirmed across 20 seeds); live Llama 3 validation achieves F1 0.928–0.949 without parameter recalibration. The faithfulness check catches 100% of controlled fabrications and 21% of real LLM magnitude-drift hallucinations. All mechanisms are mapped to EU AI Act, OCC, and MAS obligations. Code is released at https://github.com/researcher-4795/governance-control-plane.

title: Beyond skin deep: physiologic oral pigmentation as an overlooked validation gap in AI-assisted oral cancer screening
abstract: AI-assisted oral cancer screening tools, exemplified by MeMoSA, have been validated almost exclusively in Asian populations. We propose a testable hypothesis: physiologic oral pigmentation, which varies by race independent of pathology, may cause classifiers to misclassify normal variation as suspicious or miss camouflaged lesions. Following precedent from pulse oximetry and dermatology AI, we call for pigmentation-stratified validation before deployment in racially diverse settings such as the United States.

title: When Errors Have Unequal Consequences: Second-Order Complementary Log Loss for Cost-Sensitive Boosting
abstract: Multiclass decisions in finance can have sharply asymmetric consequences: reserving nothing for a loan that subsequently liquidates can be much more costly than reserving too much for a loan that repays. Standard softmax cross-entropy depends only on the probability assigned to the true class and does not encode these decision costs. We address this gap by building a cost matrix into the training loss: each possible wrong decision has its own penalty term, scaled by the consequence of that decision under the true outcome, so a decision is penalized by its estimated impact rather than by the bare fact that it differs from the true class. We adopt cost-weighted complementary log loss ( cwcl ), an established loss with a potentially asymmetric cost matrix, as an objective for second-order gradient-boosted trees. Our central contribution is its second-order treatment: the exact raw-logit gradient and diagonal Hessian, a proof of non-convexity in the logits, and a numerically stable implementation with a non-negative Hessian approximation. We also prove that the population minimizer’s highest-scoring action minimizes expected cost under the supplied matrix; cwcl ’s outputs are decision scores, not calibrated class probabilities. We evaluate loan-loss reserve decisions on 60, 176 seriously delinquent loans from Freddie Mac’s Single-Family Loan-Level Dataset, covering 2011–2015 origination vintages and a 2017 test year. We score on each loan’s subsequently realized loss. Across five training seeds, cwcl assigns a zero reserve to around 3 of the 1, 528 test loans that later liquidate, against around 29 for a direct cost regression that is trained on each loan’s own realized losses rather than on class labels. cwcl ’s mean loss is \(0.15\%\) of exposure below calibrated cross-entropy with the minimum-expected-cost decision and \(0.24\%\) above the direct regression. On a public eight-class life-insurance benchmark, cwcl gives up some accuracy and probability quality but reduces ordinal cost by \(10.1\%\) relative to cross-entropy with standard multiclass arg-max settings. These findings characterize the optimization and decision trade-offs of complementary-log boosting within the evaluated methods.

title: Semantic Credibility: Cold-Start Priors for Novel Insurance Claim Codes with LLM Embeddings
abstract: New insurance claim codes enter portfolios before code-specific outcomes are available. Classical credibility then falls back to a collective or observed parent-group estimate, leaving families absent from training undifferentiated. We introduce Semantic Credibility (SemCred), a nested estimator whose lowest rung is a code-specific prior constructed from outcomes of description-similar training codes. Family gates operate in both severity and volume channels; an own-experience gate is used only for severity, where independent claim counts support an automatic transition toward code experience. Volume remains a cold-start prior in the absence of an exogenous exposure denominator. We evaluate synthetic ICD-9 claims and real Medicare HCPCS payments using unseen-code holdouts with the family represented in training and unseen-family holdouts, hierarchy-composition tests, and a four-fold rolling backtest. Against pre-specified matched-depth fallbacks, SemCred lowers severity and expenditure log-MAE in all four dataset-regime conditions; this comparison isolates the semantic rung rather than claiming dominance over deeper hierarchies. When inserted beneath stronger prefix or ontology structures, the semantic rung matches or improves standalone accuracy, with the largest gains where hierarchy is empty or weak. A SapBERT ladder achieves temporal severity error of 1.268 versus 1.492 for hierarchical credibility, and 1.27 versus 1.51 on codes officially activated in the target year. SemCred is a traceable lower rung for code-level payment priors whose severity component retires as claims accumulate. The code is available at: https://github.com/yejining99/semcred

title: Phoenix Experiment — Grok image interactions dataset (v1.0)
abstract: A small, descriptive dataset of public exchanges on X in which the author's accounts (@BJ_Beyond, @BJ_hal) addressed @grok and an image generated by Grok appeared in the exchange. It documents a ritual convergence: over a few days Grok's image replies settled into a fixed, slot-based text template carrying author-introduced keywords. The dataset describes what was observed; it does not establish a mechanism. Window: 5 Aug – 13 Nov 2026 (53 rows), plus 2 pre-window rows (19 Apr and 1 May 2026) for context only. 55 rows; 51 Grok replies with media; 2 self-declared rows; 58 unique images. Times in Europe/Rome; latency = Grok reply time minus user post time. Limitations. Photos only: exchanges without an image are not included, so there is no denominator and no trigger rate can be estimated. Small n: 53 in-window rows over 9 days. 2 rows are self-declared Grok-made images whose prompt is not public. Human authorship of the prompts is the account owner's testimony (14 Nov 2026) and cannot be verified via the API. "Rule six" is the author's own convention, not a documented Grok or xAI feature. Statements produced by Grok are model output (claims to test), not findings. The finding is descriptive; any mechanism is a hypothesis. Part 2 (vessel test, exit, extinction) is pending. What is not included. Grok images and Grok's full reply texts are not redistributed and are not covered by the CC BY 4.0 license. Posts are referenced by X Post ID and official x.com URL; images by the SHA256 checksum of the copy archived privately by the author.

title: 标题:卦象层:一种基于《易经》二进制编码的离散瓶颈架构及其移动端验证 Title:Hexagram Layer: A Discrete Bottleneck Architecture Based on the Binary Encoding of the Book of Changes and Its Mobile Verification
abstract: 大模型连续隐状态缺少显式结构约束,容易引发语义漂移与逻辑不一致;《易经》六十四卦作为完备的6位64状态符号系统,长期局限于哲学解读,缺少可训练、可复现的计算实证。本文提出卦象层,一种融合周易卦象二进制编码的离散瓶颈可微架构。首先将六十四卦映射为6位二进制状态,对错卦、综卦、互卦、变卦四类卦变操作给出严格形式化定义,借助邻接矩阵构建卦变状态转移约束;其次提出爻象结构化初始化策略,为原型向量注入卦象先验偏置,替代传统随机初始化;推导得到结构先验有效性、判别边界迁移充分条件、粗粒化信息单调性三条理论定理。在Android移动端基于纯C++标准库完成全部前向、反向逻辑实现,不依赖深度学习框架,开展三组对照实验。实验结果表明:爻象结构化初始化能够显著加速离散瓶颈层判别边界迁移;不满足学习率充分条件时模型无法收敛;粗粒化变换符合信息单调不增规律;迭代互卦映射时观测到由既济、未济二卦构成的周期‑2极限环,该现象与《易经》以两卦收束全篇的文本特征存在观察层面的呼应。本文为传统符号文化的计算化实证提供一套可复现的实现范式。 Abstract The continuous hidden states of large‑scale models lack explicit structural constraints, which may lead to semantic drift and logical inconsistency. As a complete symbolic system with 6 bits and 64 states, the sixty‑four hexagrams in the Book of Changes have long been limited to philosophical interpretation, lacking trainable and reproducible computational evidence. This paper proposes the Hexagram Layer, a differentiable discrete‑bottleneck architecture integrated with binary encoding of I‑Ching hexagrams. Firstly, the sixty‑four hexagrams are mapped to 6‑bit binary states. Four hexagram‑transformation operations, namely inverse hexagram, reversed hexagram, mutual hexagram and changed hexagram, are formally defined, and hexagram‑transition constraints are constructed via adjacency matrix. Secondly, a hexagram‑structured initialization strategy is proposed to inject hexagram‑based prior bias into prototype vectors instead of conventional random initialization. Three theoretical theorems are derived concerning the validity of structural prior, sufficient conditions for decision‑boundary migration, and information monotonicity of coarse‑graining. All forward and backward computations are implemented purely in C++ standard library on Android mobile devices without deep‑learning frameworks, and three groups of comparative experiments are carried out. Experimental results demonstrate that hexagram‑structured initialization greatly accelerates decision‑boundary migration of the discrete bottleneck layer; the model fails to converge when the sufficient condition of learning rate is violated; coarse‑graining transformation satisfies the monotonic non‑increase property of information. A period‑2 limit cycle formed by Ji‑Ji and Wei‑Ji is observed during mutual‑hexagram iteration, which is observationally consistent with the textual feature that the Book of Changes ends with these two hexagrams. This work provides a reproducible paradigm for computational verification of traditional cultural symbols.

title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is 5.85times on Ouro-2.6B and 5.13times on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

title: Faithful by Audit: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Financial Decisions
abstract: Financial decision systems pair a tabular classifier with post-hoc feature attributions, typically SHAP over gradient-boosted trees. They report which features affected the score, not why a decision was made. Large language models can generate chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations, but fluent rationales need not be faithful. We study two high-stakes financial settings: transaction fraud detection and consumer credit risk, where the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) requires accurate adverse-action reason codes. Using LoRA fine-tuning, distillation, and DPO with faithfulness-based preferences, we construct CoT explainers for IBM TabFormer and LendingClub, and audit them with FinFaith, a unified intervention-based auditing suite. Three findings replicate across both domains. First, on identical evaluation subsamples, XGBoost consistently outperforms all CoT variants; therefore, we argue that CoT is an explanation layer, not a replacement scorer. Second, observational faithfulness is easy and interventional faithfulness is hard. The models cite features fluently and compute their arithmetic correctly 60–98% of the time, yet perturbing a cited feature changes the decision barely, more often (credit) or less often (fraud), than perturbing a feature the CoT never mentions. Third, a planted geographic cue drives up to 40% of CoT explainers’ credit decisions, yet disclosure is 0% among cases it demonstrably flipped. Faithfulness training raises interventional sensitivity, necessity from 8% to 54%, add-mistake sensitivity from 5% to 42%, but broadly rather than selectively toward what the CoT cites, and leaves the disclosure gap unclosed (cue reliance rises from 2.5% to 40.2% while confession stays at 0%). Hence, we conclude that faithfulness must be treated as an audit gate, not an assumed property, before CoT is used as a financial explanation.

title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
abstract: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter I (models, memory, skills) and a rule program p_0, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler C_θ that maps structured tasks g into new rule programs p_g. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one. Code at: https://github.com/vicgalle/craftax-program-policies

title: Evasión robusta de un clasificador comercial de detección de IA mediante un sistema generador propietario: evidencia experimental preliminar
abstract: Se evaluó, bajo protocolo de caja negra, un sistema generador de texto desarrollado íntegramente por el autor y denominado internamente Barthes Pseudomonádico KD45, frente a Pangram 4.1 — clasificador comercial de detección de texto sintético, de uso extendido en los flujos editoriales, académicos y periodísticos, y operado de forma independiente al autor. El sistema evaluado produjo tres muestras en español clasificadas con confianza del 100% como “Human Written” (n = 198, 210 y 216 tokens léxicos). Como condición de contraste, dos muestras generadas por un modelo de lenguaje de propósito general sobre premisas narrativas de complejidad equiparable fueron clasificadas con confianza del 100% como “AI Generated” (n = 377 y 324 tokens), en la misma sesión de evaluación y sin mediar ningún procedimiento de post-edición sobre ninguna de las dos condiciones. Se reporta esta discrepancia con evidencia documental directa (capturas de pantalla del clasificador) y se discuten sus implicaciones para la literatura de detección adversarial de texto sintético. Por razones de estrategia de protección de propiedad intelectual y de una eventual transacción de licenciamiento, el método generativo se reporta exclusivamente como caja negra: no se caracteriza su arquitectura, su espacio de hipótesis, ni se confirma o descarta el uso de ninguna familia de técnica conocida en la literatura de generación de lenguaje natural.

title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
abstract: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

title: AlphaLeak: What `Blind' LLM Trading Benchmarks Still See
abstract: Benchmarks often describe an LLM evaluation as blind after replacing company names and tickers with anonymous identifiers. We argue that blindness is not a preprocessing operation but an empirical property: under a declared threat model, the released record must resist linkage to its source while retaining what the benchmark means to evaluate. Our matched utility–linkability audit for point-in-time stock ranking holds the stock, date, numeric features, and realized return fixed, varying only the visible identity and news representation. An open-ended LLM, given one name-masked record (Blind) and neither a candidate list nor a corpus, names the issuer on 71% of rows; with same-date corpus access, fixed retrieval attacks recover the source on 99.8% of rows, and strict redaction, typed entity replacement, and LLM rewriting remain similarly linkable. Theme and Event abstractions cut exact-stock recovery to 5.1% and 3.9% against a 1.37% chance rate, but neither improves the Rank Information Coefficient over a numeric-only condition, so no tested representation combines near-chance linkability with detectable utility. Raw news is model- and prompt-order-sensitive and statistically unresolved within sectors; its sample portfolio difference concentrates in sector allocation without establishing within-sector selection. Separate attacks recover identity from numeric profiles and longitudinal scores even when text is masked. These surfaces motivate a threat-model-relative complete-record audit reporting source and group linkability and no-news-anchored, target-level utility. The code is available at https://github.com/minsuk-sung/ICAIF2026-AlphaLeak.

title: On Representational and Functional Alignment of Training Data Attribution Methods for Language Models
abstract: Existing approaches to training data attribution derive influence estimates from different sources of information, including gradients, model-internal states, and surface-level similarity. However, comparisons between attribution methods remain incomplete, often relying on indirect evaluations through downstream task performance. In this work, we introduce a framework for directly comparing methods along three dimensions: functional alignment, which measures correlation between full attribution vectors; representational alignment, which captures structural similarity of the representations underlying attribution; and cross-method predictability, which evaluates agreement on local pairwise ranking decisions. We observe strong representational and moderate functional alignment within paradigms. Alignment across paradigms is low and task-dependent, yet stable across models. Our results suggest that the similar downstream performance observed across paradigms in prior work can be attributed to agreement on the relative importance of documents, rather than to agreement on rankings of the full training data.

title: FAP-Bench: A Matched-Control Benchmark for Horizontal Federated Cross-Sectional Equity-Return Prediction
abstract: Institutions that each hold part of the equity market’s history cannot pool it. FAP-Bench measures what they give up by training a return-prediction model together instead, exchanging model updates and, to standardize inputs, monthly aggregate histograms. It is a controlled laboratory for horizontal federation rather than a model of any particular consortium. It prices the coordination cost of that restriction, not the privacy it buys: clients are stylized industry splits of one licensed panel, and privacy is priced at a single differential-privacy setting. The benchmark builds a 3.27M firm-month panel from CRSP and Compustat over 1964–2023, splits it into twelve industry clients, and runs centralized, local-only and three federated rules at a matched compute budget. Every configuration publishes the smallest gap it can resolve before any method is ranked, and every heterogeneity treatment is paired with a control that imposes the same aggregate burden evenly, so the difference isolates cross-client structure. Two findings. First, a coordination cost appears in the one configuration where the model resolves more signal. On seven characteristics, where the network resolves little signal, no rule separates from pooling economically. On twenty, where the model resolves substantially more signal, the two averaging rules give up accuracy that the cell does resolve (Rank IC, q < 0.02). They also show a net Sharpe shortfall that it does not resolve, which we report as a bound. An adaptive server optimizer stays level with pooling on both, but its server step size was searched and the pooled model’s optimizer was not, so this does not show that it matches an equally tuned pooled model. Both configurations resolve gaps of comparable size, so this is a difference in effect, not in power. Two configurations cannot establish a trend, and they differ in panel width, network size and client learning rate at once, so the cost cannot be attributed to any one of these. Swapping the network for ridge also changes which rule pays, so no ranking among the rules holds across model classes. Second, heterogeneity in what a client holds clears the benchmark’s noise floor, while heterogeneity in how it participates almost never does. The participation side is measured mostly on 60 test months, where our intervals are somewhat too narrow, and only one of its three treatments is rechecked on 408. Most economic differences sit below what this data can resolve, so we report magnitudes as bounds rather than estimates.

title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
abstract: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
abstract: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

title: Neylira-Φ: Recurrent Optimization Curves and Certified Recursive Learning - Sharp Thresholds, Exact Finite-Observation Limits, and Compositional Certificates for AI Recursive Self-Improvement
authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki
abstract: Neylira-Φ is a self-contained mathematical research monograph connecting the geometry of optimization trajectories, fundamental limits of finite observations, and structural certificates for accepted changes to a learning system. This release contains the complete 81-page expanded manuscript, including 48 pages devoted to AI recursive self-improvement, together with editable LaTeX, reference implementations, exact rational and symbolic verification programs, figures, audit records, and structured research data. The central question is how to distinguish apparent progress from a mathematically certified improvement in a learning procedure. A decreasing loss curve can repeatedly violate discrete convexity, and even exact finite loss-and-gradient observations can fail to determine whether those violations will persist indefinitely. Nevertheless, explicit assumptions on update operators, task comparisons, evaluation procedures, and computational costs can certify particular modifications. The manuscript develops both sides of this distinction: impossibility results for observation alone, and constructive guarantees for structurally certified changes. 1. Sharp recurrence for constant-step gradient descent For every normalized constant step h = eta*L satisfying 7/4 < h < 2, the manuscript constructs a globally smooth, strongly convex scalar C(1,1) objective with a convergent gradient-descent trajectory and infinitely many strictly negative second differences of the objective values. Here C(1,1) means continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz gradient. The construction has an exact scaled return. With the minimum normalized to zero, a period P and contraction factor 0 < R < 1 satisfy: x[k+P] = R*x[k] f(x[k+P]) = R²*f(x[k]) At infinitely many designated indices: f(x[k]) − 2*f(x[k+1]) + f(x[k+2]) < 0 Thus the objective remains strongly convex and the loss decreases, while the sequence of loss values repeatedly fails discrete convexity. The exact return identity establishes persistence over infinitely many cycles. The universal convexity theorem for h ≤ 7/4 is established prior work, reproduced with attribution to Barzilai, Shamir, and Zamani. Together with that lower-range theorem, the construction gives the sharp recurrence-existence boundary within the stated strict stability interval. The manuscript also distinguishes regularity classes. Under the specified positive-definite linearization and strict stability assumptions, differentiability of the gradient at the limiting minimizer forces eventual recovery of loss-curve convexity. Analytic approximations can preserve arbitrarily long prescribed finite patterns of violations. This does not assert infinite recurrence for one analytic objective under a constant gradient step. 2. Exact finite observations do not identify the eventual regime An explicit quadratic-core patch modifies the objective in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of its minimizer. Two compensating moment conditions preserve both function values and gradients outside the modified core. For every prescribed finite exact observation transcript of the recurrent construction, an eventually recovering companion can therefore match that transcript while preserving the declared smoothness and strong-convexity bounds, minimizer, minimum value, and initial gap. The quantifiers matter: each finite transcript admits a suitable companion; a single recovering objective is not claimed to match the entire infinite recurrent orbit. In the stated promised family and exact point-oracle model, this yields impossibility results for always-terminating deterministic classifiers and almost-surely finite randomized classifiers, including procedures with adaptive query locations. Randomization does not provide a worst-case success guarantee strictly above one half over the entire family. These results concern finite point observations; symbolic descriptions and additional structural assumptions can supply information beyond that oracle model. 3. A necessary and sufficient criterion for arbitrary positive-definite switching For positive-definite quadratic tasks, the manuscript derives an exact universal loss-curve convexity criterion for arbitrary symmetric positive-definite optimizer switching. The normalized update matrices may fail to commute; simultaneous diagonalization is not assumed. If their spectra lie in [a,b], with 0 < a ≤ b < 2, define: rho = max(abs(1−a), abs(1−b)) nu = distance from 0 to the interval [1−b,1−a] Gamma = 1 − rho²*(2 − nu²) Universal loss-sequence convexity in this class holds if and only if Gamma ≥ 0. The bounds concern the energy-normalized update matrices. A strict positive margin supports the stated local nonlinear extension under the required remainder and domain conditions. An explicit analytic example with alternating step sizes shows why the equality boundary Gamma = 0 cannot generally inherit that nonlinear guarantee. The manuscript also supplies an exact recurrent construction with noncommuting updates outside the admissible switching region. 4. Exact burst lengths and asymptotic event densities For the contraction-ratio model E[k+1] = q[k]*E[k], where q[k] lies in [a,b] and 0 ≤ a ≤ b < 1, the manuscript determines the largest possible number of consecutive strict negative second differences and the maximal asymptotic frequency of those events. Define: Delta = 1/(1−b) − 1/(1−a) M = max(0, ceil(Delta) − 1) The exact maximum consecutive burst length is M, and the maximal asymptotic event density is M/(M+1). Explicit periodic constructions attain both bounds. The strict integer boundary is part of the result. These theorems classify the declared contraction-ratio model. They do not claim to solve the optimal consecutive-violation geometry of every fixed-step gradient-descent problem. A scalar-quadratic corollary gives exact burst thresholds under bounded relative-gradient errors. 5. Constructive progress observers and task interpretation Every Schur-stable linear update map admits a computable positive-definite observer with any prescribed finite order of positive alternating differences. The construction selects an observer for the requested finite order; it does not require one observer to control every order simultaneously. The manuscript gives finite computation procedures, nonnormal examples, perturbation budgets, and extensions to the stated nonlinear and changing-map settings. Established Lyapunov and hypercontraction ideas are attributed. A comparison bridge connects observer-energy control to an external task, making explicit what must be established before internal progress implies protected-task improvement. 6. Compositional guarantees for accepted recursive improvements The 48-page recursive self-improvement part develops a conditional mathematical framework for changing optimizers, representations, objectives, and evaluation procedures while tracking accumulated errors and costs. If accepted changes satisfy: v[j+1] ≤ r[j]*v[j] + d[j] their exact propagated certificate is: v[N] ≤ (product of r[j] for j = 0,...,N−1)v[0]+ sum over i = 0,...,N−1 ofd[i](product of r[j] for j = i+1,...,N−1) An empty product equals 1. This expression separates contraction from approximation error, representation-transfer error, and objective drift. Further results connect changing internal certificates to a fixed protected residual, give retention bounds for task families, and describe when the accumulated guarantee remains meaningful. Fresh-data, anytime-valid promotion tests and inherited error budgets control false promotions across indefinitely many adaptive proposals under the stated conditional-validity assumptions. A claim that every committed version improves protected population utility requires evidence covering every commitment. The framework guarantees properties of accepted changes satisfying its assumptions; it does not guarantee an unlimited supply of beneficial proposals. 7. Computational benefit includes proposal and validation costs The manuscript separates iteration-count improvements from improvements in actual work. A certified target-time advantage requires an upper work bound for the candidate, including proposal and evaluation overhead, below a lower work bound for the baseline from the same checkpoint to the same target. An exact worked example reduces total assigned work from 66 to 40 units, including 20 units of proposal and validation overhead. For a less demanding target, the same modification instead costs 28 units against the baseline’s 22. These calculations demonstrate a precise payback condition within an explicit mathematical cost model. They are theoretical cost comparisons; practical neural-network speedups require measurement. Research significance The manuscript provides a mathematical connection between observational nonidentifiability and constructive certification of self-modification. It identifies what a finite training history cannot establish and specifies additional conditions under which individual learning-system changes can be accepted with compositional guarantees. Potential applications include learning-curve interpretation, optimizer selection, protected-task retention, adaptive evaluation, and research on certified recursive learning. The contribution combines explicit constructions, sharp classifications in declared models, and conditional certificate composition. Applying the framework to large neural networks requires evidence that its assumptions and cost comparisons hold in those systems. Verification and reproducibility All 11 supplied finite audit programs and the executable example printed in the manuscript passed in the original reproduction record and in a fresh packaging run on a disposable copy. title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
abstract: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

title: Perfilado Epistémico y Señales Honestas Costosas: Hacia una Metodología Forense
abstract: Authorship attribution and the profiling of anonymous actors in complex digital and forensic environments are undergoing an irreversible epistemological crisis. Traditional methodologies—grounded in lexical and syntactic stylometry, code analysis, infrastructure metadata, and temporal patterns—prove deeply vulnerable against adversaries equipped with high operational security (OPSEC) discipline. This paper posits that digital forensics, open-source intelligence (OSINT), and criminal analysis must abandon low-friction indicators (when confronting sophisticated adversaries) as these belong to the economic category of "Cheap Talk." As its core methodological contribution, this article introduces the framework of Epistemic Profiling driven by Costly Cognitive Signals (Cognitive Proof-of-Work). Grounded in the Handicap Principle from evolutionary biology, information economics, and computational cryptography, the model contends that the key to attribution lies not in the generic amount of knowledge required, but in deciphering the actor’s theoretical framework, mental heuristics, and problem-solving system. By auditing how an individual decomposes, approaches, and resolves a challenge under pressure—demonstrating that an actor linked to a specific educational, generational, and/or cultural background will solve the exact same problem in a characteristic and structurally distinct manner from another, regardless of using identical contemporary tools—the analyst isolates the traces of an inalienable "doctrinal ecosystem." This enables the construction of a rigorous educational, institutional, and geographic profile of an anonymous actor, both in exploratory investigative scenarios and in filtering processes across bounded sets of candidates.

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.

title: Finite-Sample Recovery of Predictive History Quotients from Independent POMDP Trajectories
abstract: We study a modest but identifiable abstraction problem for partially observed control: under one fixed data-collection policy, which bounded observation contexts have the same finite-horizon continuation law? We define the *episode-position predictive quotient*, an explicitly policy- and position-dependent estimand. Our estimator first selects contexts on one half of independently reset trajectories, then takes at most one prespecified continuation block from each trajectory in the other half. It compares fixed- alphabet histograms by empirical total variation and abstains whenever a pair lacks the samples required by its own concentration bound. Under an $`\varepsilon`$-gap, a per-context visitation floor, and a selection threshold no larger than the inference threshold, we prove exact recovery with probability $`1-\delta`$ from $`O((d+\log(K/\delta))/(\mu_{\min}\varepsilon^2))`$ trajectories, where $`d`$ is the continuation-alphabet size and $`K`$ the selected context count. A two-point construction shows the dependence on $`\mu_{\min}`$ and $`\varepsilon`$ is unavoidable; the dependence on $`d`$ is not matched and is known to be improvable by optimal closeness testers. The guarantee is non-asymptotic: it does not treat overlapping windows as independent, does not rely on chi-square calibration, and conditions each context only on its own count, so nested candidate contexts are covered. Implementation checks on three analytically solvable environments—each with $`\varepsilon`$ set below its known gap—recover the exact quotients on all of 20 seeds, including an environment whose quotient requires merging; a budget sweep shows the power gate degrading through abstention with no incorrect merge at any budget; and a position-nonstationary chain shows the overlapping-window mode systematically merging contexts the episode-position quotient separates.

title: Don’t Trust, Verify: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Engineering for Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Feature engineering in tabular fraud detection is critical yet challenging to automate due to extreme class imbalance, which heavily penalizes spurious features. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate candidate features from dataset schemas, schema-level plausibility correlates poorly with actual predictive value. We propose an LLM-based Automated Feature Engineering (AutoFE) framework that assesses candidates strictly on executed empirical behavior. Every candidate is executed on a data split to extract a structured profile of empirical metrics, including deterministic data-integrity checks and output value distributions. A role-separated multi-agent panel, comprising a Critic, Proposer, and Adjudicator, evaluates this evidence to rigorously retain, repair, or discard features. Because the optimal interpretation of raw diagnostics is unknown a priori, a single evaluation pass is insufficient. To bridge this gap, a validation-gated meta-learning stage optimizes the system iteratively across multiple execution passes. By analyzing the realized downstream utility of previously accepted features, this stage dynamically refines the natural-language skills used to read diagnostic tools, updates system memory regarding feature-family behavior, and recalibrates acceptance thresholds for subsequent passes. Evaluated on three severely imbalanced fraud benchmarks (CCF, TabFormer, BAF v2), our framework achieves the strongest PR-AUC among the evaluated LLM-based methods while retaining compact feature sets. By consolidating the evaluation process, moving from iterative, trial-and-error prompting to a single, comprehensive diagnostic profile, the method reduces per-pass evaluation costs by 42% while significantly lifting predictive performance, including a PR-AUC increase from 0.878 to 0.949 on the CCF dataset.

title: The Alert-Feedback Trap: Why Drift-Adaptive Fraud Detectors Fail Under Realistic Label Feedback, and How Much Exploration It Takes to Escape
abstract: Financial-crime detectors must adapt to drift, but in deployment they are retrained almost entirely on the labels their own alerts produce: only flagged transactions are investigated and labeled. We characterize the resulting failure mode, the alert-feedback trap. On the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset, detectors across linear, tree-ensemble, and graph-neural-network families collapse under a regime change (illicit-class F1 from 0.91 to 0.03), though ranking degrades far less than fixed-threshold metrics suggest. Under alert-only feedback, drift-adaptive learners that update from a recent window of alert-selected labels are trapped: a strong detector that catches 113 of 169 illicit transactions while frozen falls to 93 when it adapts on its own alerts—worse than freezing in all 200 bootstrap resamples and under every gate setting we tried—and a collapsed detector recovers only 9–30, versus 98 under bulk feedback. The trap is an interaction of selection bias and forgetting, not an inevitability of alert-only feedback: a practitioner baseline that retrains on the full label history plus the alert labels escapes it under the same feedback (113 → 130; collapsed 14 → 79), while the same alert labels without the history do not (74; 46). Off-policy ϵ -exploration, by contrast, is not a reliable escape once data variability is accounted for. We release a prequential protocol with delayed, budgeted, selection-biased feedback.

title: BINA Theory: A Four-State Conceptual Framework for Information Representation
abstract: BINA Theory is a four-state conceptual framework for representing information, evidence, and evaluation. It defines four distinct symbolic states: -1 (Opposed or Rejected), -0 (Unknown or Insufficient Evidence), 0 (Neutral), and 1 (Supported). Its central distinction is that -0 and 0 represent different informational conditions. This record documents the foundational definitions and currently established symbolic representation of the framework. This is a foundational conceptual record, not a claim of experimentally verified superiority or a completed formal logic system.

title: CARGO: Credit Action Recourse via Regulation-Bounded, Graph-Constrained Ordered Planning
abstract: Lenders are required to disclose the principal reasons for a credit denial, and recent guidance asks that those reasons be specific enough to act on. This requirement points to recourse , the actionable steps that turn a denial into an approval. Existing explanation and recourse methods operate at the level of individual features. Attribution methods such as SHAP and LIME report influential features rather than actions an applicant can take, counterfactual methods compute feature changes that rarely map to real actions, responsiveness scores assemble no plan when no single feature responds, and none of them accounts for actions that depend on one another. We propose CARGO (Credit Action Recourse via Regulation-Bounded, Graph-Constrained Ordered Planning), which builds recourse from actions rather than individual features. CARGO fixes a catalog of credit actions matched to the reason codes lenders already file, arranges them in a constraint graph of precedence and exclusion edges with a per-applicant applicability filter, and searches for the ordered feasible plan most likely to reverse each denial. Disclosure practice reports at most four reasons per notice, and CARGO adopts this cap of four actions per plan. One plan then serves both audiences, executable recourse for the applicant and verified reason codes for the lender’s notice. In experiments on nine dataset–model cells, CARGO achieves the highest executable recovery on eight, raising it by up to 28.6 points compared to the best competitor while returning no infeasible plan, and recovers up to \(97\%\) of the applicants whom single-feature methods abandon. Ablations show that the action catalog and the constraint graph each contribute to this improvement.

title: CGGS: Confidence-Guided Graph Sampling for Scalable GNN Fraud Detection on Imbalanced Financial Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a powerful paradigm for financial fraud detection by exploiting the relational structure of transaction networks to identify suspicious behaviour and coordinated fraud. Translating them into a viable production system, however, remains hard under strict memory, compute and latency budget – costs that span the entire model lifecycle, not merely GNN training. A real transaction graph of hundreds of millions of accounts is overwhelmingly a graph of benign nodes, so much of that lifecycle budget is spent processing nodes that carry little discriminative signal. The same benign majority drives a second challenge, fraud-class homophily collapse : because fraudsters deliberately interact with legitimate entities to camouflage and evade detection, the proportion of same-class edges incident on fraud nodes drops and the fraud class is driven into high heterophily, so neighbourhood aggregation averages the fraud signal away while imbalance biases the classifier toward the benign majority. We propose CGGS ( C onfidence- G uided G raph S ampling), a two-stage framework that turns both liabilities into a single opportunity at no additional compute cost. Stage 1 trains a lightweight tabular scorer – gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) in our instantiation – on the node features, ranking every candidate entity by fraud probability without touching graph topology. Stage 2 prunes the confidently-benign entities before the graph is assembled, so the GNN trains only on the compact, higher-homophily subgraph of uncertain, high-risk, and informative nodes. We prove that confidence-guided pruning increases the expected fraud-class homophily and reduces the effective imbalance ratio under a mild ranking assumption. Experiments on a production-scale proprietary transaction graph and two public benchmarks show that CGGS reduces graph size and lifecycle computational cost while outperforming full-graph training and alternative pruning strategies, with ablations confirming robustness across pruning thresholds.

title: Data and code for input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift in water-pollution incident classification
abstract: Reproducibility package for the manuscript “Input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift: An evaluation of water-pollution incident classifiers”. This retrospective study evaluates 1,648 compiled incident records (2004–2024), retaining all four recorded severity grades: 1,375 minor, 188 moderate, 61 major and 24 exceptionally major records. The predictor audit restricts 27 candidate fields to 15 retrospective inputs. Evaluation includes grouped nested validation, three forward-time windows and two basin holdouts, with feature selection confined to training partitions. S1_Data_and_code.zip contains the original Excel snapshot, processed tables, field and duplicate audits, executable Python analysis, environment specifications, fold assignments, record-level predictions, feature-selection records, bootstrap outputs and figures. README_data_and_code.md describes reproduction, provenance and limitations. Archive size: 12,784,439 bytes. SHA-256: 2ef99d08ec200ac0376e3822e10183b3cd9729f706fbe8a1a7b22b4bb9396d01. An earlier source compilation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20426262. That record contains an older, different analysis and is not the archive of this four-level study. The present package preserves the new four-level analysis and its validation outputs. Limitations: original incident notices, complete meteorological product documentation and label-adjudication records are unavailable in the supplied compilation. Candidate incident groups are not verified unique event identifiers. Computational reproducibility does not establish the authenticity, accuracy or prospective availability of the original observations. This is not a validated emergency prediction product. Third-party dependencies and the TabICLv2 checkpoint retain their own licenses; model weights are not relicensed by this record. OpenAI Codex assisted planning, code, checking, visualization, interpretation and writing; no incident observations were generated. Authors remain responsible for verification and scientific claims. Authors: Ruidong Chen, Xin Zhao, Dapeng Deng, Yongmei Wang and Jie Tang, Anhui Agricultural University. Funding: National Key Research and Development Program of China (2023YFC3205701) and Cultivated Land Quality Big Data Platform Service Project (HX20250744), both awarded to Yongmei Wang. The authors declare no competing financial or non-financial interests.

title: From Features to Circuits: Mechanistic Interpretability for Financial Tabular Transformers
abstract: The financial sector relies on structured tabular data, which has led to the adoption of machine learning models for regression and classification tasks, including credit scoring, fraud detection, and risk assessment. Transformer-based architectures have recently shown competitive performance on tabular data, yet their internal computations remain opaque, limiting adoption in heavily regulated domains, such as finance. Responsible deployment requires predictions to be explainable, both to meet regulatory obligations and to give practitioners confidence in model outputs. We present a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies the sparse computational subgraphs, i.e., circuits, through which a tabular transformer processes individual input features. We perform empirical analysis on a range of real-world financial datasets and show that discovered circuits are sparse, faithful, and feature-specific, providing a foundation for explainable AI in financial domains.

title: What Makes a Financial Benchmark Financial? A Role-Conditioned Audit of Faithfulness and Capability
abstract: Financial question answering and hallucination benchmarks are often treated as evidence of professional financial capability. We audit four financial benchmarks and show that surface financial complexity and audited capability profiles often diverge: two of the three faithfulness benchmarks are strongly label-separable from partial inputs, and the role-conditioned audit assigns all items in these three benchmarks to lookup, textual synthesis, or grounded calculation. We introduce AURUM, a role-conditioned audit framework that combines construction diagnostics with a finance-oriented capability ontology aligned with professional financial workflows, and use it to derive reporting and construction guidelines for future financial benchmarks. Independent expert review of 120 held-out items yielded 89% exact agreement with AURUM.
